query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting the heavy Hf component in as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with a lighter refractory element, namely vanadium, will reduce overall alloy density without sacrificing its high room‐ and elevated‐temperature strengths.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr, which has an approximate density of 10.21 g/cm³, a room‐temperature yield strength of ~1600 MPa, and a high‐temperature (e.g., 1000 °C) yield strength of ~855 MPa.
generation.intervention: Replace Hf with an equiatomic amount of vanadium to form a VMoTaTiZr alloy, keeping the other elements unchanged.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests performed on as‐cast samples at room temperature (around 25 °C) and at 1000 °C under comparable loading rates (e.g., quasi-static tensile/compressive conditions) to the baseline studies.
generation.structural_mediator: The chemical substitution is expected to maintain the underlying single-phase or solid-solution body‐centered cubic structure, thereby preserving the key dislocation-based and precipitation-related strengthening mechanisms while lowering the overall mass.
generation.mechanism: Vanadium, being significantly lighter than hafnium yet still a refractory element, should reduce the alloy’s density by lowering its average atomic mass. Its similar valence and refractory nature are anticipated to maintain the dislocation mobility and slip system interactions that underpin both room‐ and high‐temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The VMoTaTiZr alloy will exhibit a reduced density (targeting roughly a 10% reduction relative to 10.21 g/cm³) while achieving room-temperature yield strengths near 1600 MPa and high-temperature (1000 °C) yield strengths around 855 MPa, with fracture toughness and ductility remaining comparable to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: HfMoTaTiZr as-cast alloy with density ~10.21 g/cm³, ~1600 MPa yield strength at room temperature, and ~855 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to the as-cast condition, with mechanical testing at room temperature (~25 °C) and at an elevated temperature of 1000 °C under quasi-static loading; microstructural integrity is assumed to be similar between the baseline and the modified alloy.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how fully replacing Hf with V may affect other performance metrics such as room-temperature fracture toughness or subtle microstructural characteristics (e.g., precipitate distribution) that also contribute to mechanical behavior. Further investigation may be needed to optimize the substitution level.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate an alloy with the composition VMoTaTiZr by replacing Hf in the baseline HfMoTaTiZr with vanadium using arc melting to produce as-cast samples. Measure density via Archimedes’ method and perform standardized mechanical testing (tensile/compressive tests) at room temperature (≈25 °C) and at 1000 °C under quasi-static loading.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength and ductility (target ~1600 MPa and comparable ductility metrics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the V-substituted alloy fails to reduce the density by at least ~5-10% relative to 10.21 g/cm³, or if either the room-temperature or high-temperature yield strength decreases by more than 10% relative to the HfMoTaTiZr baseline (or if fracture toughness is significantly degraded), the hypothesis is falsified.

Supporting data for senary refractory high-entropy alloy CrxMoNbTaVW

Abstract: This data article is related to the research paper entitled “senary refractory high-entropy alloy CrxMoNbTaVW [1]”. In this data article, the pseudo-binary Cr-MoNbTaVW phase diagram is presented to show the impact of Cr content to the senary Cr-MoNbTaVW alloy system; the sub-lattice site fractions are presented to show the disordered property of the Cr-MoNbTaVW BCC structures; the equilibrium and Scheil solidification results with the actual sample elemental compositions are presented to show the thermodynamic information of the melted/solidified CrxMoNbTaVW samples; and the raw EDS scan data of the arc-melted CrxMoNbTaVW samples are also provided.

Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
